Let’s talk about Chapter 9 — Sustaining Change: Preventing Relapse and Embracing Growth.
You know, change isn’t usually a straight path. Even after you’ve made real progress, those old habits can sneak back in—especially when life gets stressful or you’re facing a big transition.
Think of it like tending a garden. Your new growth thrives with regular care, but if you’re not paying attention, weeds can pop up when you least expect them.
So, how do you keep moving forward?
Here are a few strategies to help you hold onto your momentum:
First, keep an eye on your triggers. Be alert to the situations or relationships that tend to bring those old lifetraps back to life. Notice the early warning signs—maybe it’s a familiar wave of emotion, or that urge to withdraw, overcompensate, or just give in.
Next, make it a habit to review your progress. Take some time now and then to look back at how far you’ve come. Celebrate your wins, big or small, and notice where those old patterns still try to sneak in. This shifts your focus to growth, instead of chasing perfection.
Don’t forget to revisit your tools. The things that helped you before—like journaling, practicing self-compassion, setting boundaries, or reaching out for support—these aren’t one-and-done fixes. They’re lifelong practices you can always come back to.
And let’s be real—setbacks will happen. Expect them. But when they do, try to respond with patience and curiosity, not self-blame. Ask yourself, “What brought this on? What can I learn for next time?” It’s all part of the process.
Staying connected is key, too. Change is so much easier when you’ve got support. Keep nurturing relationships with people who encourage your growth and gently challenge those old patterns when they show up.
Here’s a real-life example. Imagine someone who’s worked hard to overcome a social exclusion lifetrap. During a rough patch, those old feelings of isolation might bubble up again. Instead of falling back into old habits and withdrawing, they might reach out to a friend or join a group activity—using the very tools they’ve been practicing.
Sustaining change is really about creating a new normal. It’s not about making lifetraps disappear forever, but learning to spot them and manage them so they don’t run the show.
Growth becomes part of your everyday life—not just a finish line you’re trying to reach.
